transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-02-14
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Anika Patel (Redwood SA), Oliver Grant (SablePoint CTO), Priya Singh (Securty), Marcus Lee (Platform), Nina Park (Legal)

Summary:
Quick intake to understand SablePoint's security constraints for adding Redwood inference into their checkout and merchant support flows. Main themes: SOC2/ISO evidence, SSO/SAML + SCIM, RBAC model, audit logs retention and export, encryption/KMS and HSM, data residency and retention policy, and whether Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private is required.

Topics:
- Compliance standing and audit evidence requested
- Authentication, SSO, and account provisioning (SAML, SCIM)
- Encryption at rest and key management (KMS/HSM) options
- Audit logs: retention, access, export, SIEM integration
- Data residency and data retention policies / deletion workflows
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs for risk profile and cost

Action items (captured): see metadata field for owners/due dates

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'll kick us off. We wanted to learn more about your security and compliance requirements to help recommend a hosting path — Hosted, Dedicated or Private. Who wants to start with current posture?
[00:12] Oliver Grant: Yeah, sure. I can — I'm Oliver, CTO. So SablePoint handles payment orchestration and some PII, we are SOC2 Type II in progress, ISO is on roadmap. Priya here is our head of security. Our basic ask is we need clear evidence of encryption, KMS, and audit trails. We also need SSO/SAML and RBAC into any vendor console.
[00:32] Priya Singh: And one clarification — for payment tokenization flows we need no unredacted card data to leave our environment; anything sent to inference endpoints should be masked. We also want a long retention of audit logs for 3 years for forensic needs.
[00:50] Diego Ramos: Got it, thanks. Quick interrupt — when you say "no unredacted card data", do you currently tokenize before sending to external services or are you wanting the vendor to provide tokenization?
[00:58] Marcus Lee: We tokenize in our gateway yes, but we sometimes call out to a model for classification and enrichment; those payloads can inadvertently include merchant identifiers, customer name. So we need to make sure PII is either masked, redacted or never logged.
[01:14] Maya Chen: Totally, and that aligns with our controls. For Hosted we have tokenization guidance and recommend prefix-KV caching disabled for PII-heavy calls. We also offer Dedicated which gives you isolated GPU pools and no shared instance tenancy, and Private (VPC or on-prem) where the inference plane runs in your VPC and keys are in your KMS.
[01:35] Nina Park: From legal perspective, we want a binding data processing addendum and the ability to audit. Is Redwood open to onsite audits or SOC2 review processes?
[01:45] Anika Patel: We do offer SOC 2 Type II reports and can arrange for a security questionnaire and security pack. Onsite audits typically need a contracted arrangement; usually customers prefer SOC2 plus targeted attestation and a controls walkthrough.
[02:02] Priya Singh: Can you confirm encryption at rest for Hosted? Who manages the keys?
[02:08] Diego Ramos: For Hosted, encryption at rest is enforced; keys are managed by Redwood cloud KMS by default. We support customer-managed keys via cloud KMS integrations for Dedicated and Private, and for Private/on-prem we can integrate with HSMs if required. There's a little nuance: Hosted with CMK is possible for certain plans but you still rely on network tenancy of Redwood — Dedicated gives stronger tenant isolation.
[02:31] Oliver Grant: If we do CMKs, can we have key rotation logs and separation of duties, e.g., our security team holds rotation privileges?
[02:40] Diego Ramos: Yes, with customer-managed keys the key policies in KMS determine admin/grantee roles — you can set rotation and Cloud Audit logs capture key usage. With Private you get full control over KMS/HSM.
[02:51] Priya Singh: Audit logs — we need deep retention and SIEM export, preferably real-time feeds to our Splunk instance. Does Redwood support streaming audit logs to customer SIEM?
[03:02] Anika Patel: Yes, we provide audit log exports and can ship logs to your S3 bucket or push to syslog/HTTPS endpoints. For Hosted there's a standard retention (90 days) but we have add-on packages for extended retention and direct exports. For Dedicated/Private, retention and export are configurable and typically handled in-customer's storage or via dedicated log exporters.
[03:22] Marcus Lee: About RBAC — we need to sync our IdP to provision roles. Does Redwood support SAML + SCIM for provisioning and role sync?
[03:31] Diego Ramos: We support SAML SSO for console access and SCIM for group provisioning. The RBAC model supports role templates: viewer, operator, admin, and you can map IdP groups to these. There are also token scopes for API credentials so you can enforce least privilege.
[03:48] Priya Singh: Great. Also, are there separate audit trails for API calls vs console actions? We need to show who did what and the associated request payloads (redacted).
[03:57] Maya Chen: Yes, we separate control plane logs (console, IAM) and data-plane logs (inference requests). For Hosted we redact PII in logs by default and have a policy to avoid storing full request payloads unless consented. For Dedicated/Private you can choose to persist raw request logs in your own storage.
[04:15] Oliver Grant: Hmm, the default redaction — can we prove it? Is it supplanter randomization or deterministic? We need to show how redaction is performed for audits.
[04:25] Diego Ramos: We have a redaction pipeline that scrubs defined sensitive patterns and can be configured with custom rules. For audit evidence, we can provide sampling and policies. We'll include a brief doc and some examples in the pack.
[04:39] Priya Singh: Data residency — we have EU and US merchant data; some datasets cannot leave EU. If we used Hosted in US regions only, that's a blocker. What are Redwood's region controls?
[04:50] Anika Patel: Redwood Hosted supports region selection for model endpoints and we have EU regions. For stricter guarantees we recommend Dedicated pinned to an EU region or Private VPC in your region; that gives you full data egress control.
[05:06] Nina Park: For legal, retention and deletion — we need data deletion on contract termination and documented deletion workflow. How long does Redwood retain backups and are there any orphaned data copies?
[05:16] Maya Chen: Deletion policies are documented; for Hosted we have retention that depends on config — logs and telemetry typically 90 days unless you purchase extended retention. For Dedicated/Private your storage retention is customer-controlled. For contract terminations, we run scrubbing and can provide certificates of destruction on request. We'll include the process in the packet.
[05:33] Marcus Lee: We also have a question about model artifacts and weights. If we host a private model in Dedicated, do you keep copies or push them to our infra? We need assurance that model snapshots won't be used elsewhere.
[05:43] Diego Ramos: Good point. For Dedicated you can pin a model and we isolate the runtime and cache. Model files for proprietary customer models are treated as customer-owned assets and can be deployed into your Private instance. We have options to sign an NDA and contractual terms around IP.
[05:57] Oliver Grant: What about penetration testing and vulnerability disclosure? We run quarterly pentests — we'll want to coordinate.
[06:03] Anika Patel: We can coordinate red team/pen tests for Private deployments. For Hosted/Dedicated we publish a vulnerability disclosure process and have an SLA for triage.
[06:12] Priya Singh: OK, budgeting/ops question — what's the cost delta between Hosted with CMK vs Dedicated? We know it's higher but need a ballpark for comparison against our compliance needs.
[06:21] Maya Chen: High-level, Dedicated often runs 2-4x Hosted per predictable throughput, but you gain tenant isolation and stronger SLA. Private is higher still, largely one-time infra ops plus license. We'll share an indicative cost sheet after this call.
[06:35] Marcus Lee: On the technical side, we'd like a short deep-dive on networking — firewall rules, private endpoints, egress IPs. Diego can you show a sample network diagram?
[06:44] Diego Ramos: Absolutely — I'll prepare a VPC peering diagram, NAT egress patterns, and how we route inference traffic. For Private we can do private endpoint and no public internet access.
[06:55] Nina Park: For compliance reviews, can we get a mapping to our internal control IDs? We like to map vendor controls to our SOC2 framework.
[07:03] Anika Patel: We'll include a control mapping matrix (Redwood controls -> SOC2/ISO 27001) in the packet.
[07:10] Oliver Grant: One last technical detail — are KV/prefix caches flushed on tenant deletion and are there guarantees no stale secrets remain in caches?
[07:19] Diego Ramos: Cache eviction and TTL policies are part of the runtime; for Dedicated/Private we provide explicit cache wipe on deprovision and can certificate it. For Hosted we have lifecycle controls and logs demonstrating eviction. We'll add a note to the doc.
[07:34] Priya Singh: Great, thank you. Next steps recap?
[07:39] Maya Chen: Recap: we'll send SOC2/ISO summary and security pack; Diego to prepare Private/Dedicated network diagram; Anika to include controls mapping and log export options; Marcus/Priya will fill out security questionnaire and decide whether to pursue a short Dedicated benchmark.
[07:56] Oliver Grant: Sounds good. Also include a sample DPA and any addenda for data residency.
[08:03] Nina Park: We'll review and come back with a proposed timeline — target POC by end of Q1.
[08:10] Maya Chen: Perfect. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up by email.

[08:20] -- call winds down, participants still chatting about scheduling and internal owners.

Notes on transcript quality: occasional overlap, some product names transcribed inconsistent (e.g., "KV cache" as "K V cache"), minor filler words.
